title: Stephen King takes 45 years to write ONE story
html:
Hi Reader,

If you’ve ever felt bad about procrastination or missing a deadline, take note from Mr. King.

He’s in the middle of plugging his new collection of short stories, You Like It Darker, this summer.

He started writing one short story in the collection when he was a sprightly 30-year-old horror writer.

Now King, aged 76, is publishing Answer Man as part of his new collection.

King told NPR about the 45-year gap:

“I will write stories and they don’t always get done. And the ones that don’t get done go in a drawer, and I forget all about them.”

Every writer has a drawer (digital or otherwise) full of abandoned projects and manuscripts, but how many writers spend a whopping 16,425+ days on a creative project?

Ok, clearly, King wasn’t working on this story the entire time…

He only finished writing the story after his nephew John found an early draft and told King it was good.

(It’s amusing to think King still reacts to encouragement considering all of his big hits and accolades.)

But King had similar doubts about two other big hits. His wife fished an early draft of his first novel, Carrie, out from the waste paper bin in his office and told him he was onto something.

That book launched his author career.

Later, King stuffed a draft Pet Sematary in a drawer, thinking the story about an ancient burial ground and creepy dead cats who come back to life was awful.

He only published that book as part of a contractual obligation with an old publishing company. Pet Sematary went on to become a 1983 best-seller. Alas, the 2019 movie was trash.

Delaying publication for 45 years isn’t the best way to get paid to write short stories. Most writers need to spend more time publishing and less time revising. But King can still claim to be one of the most prolific modern-day authors. He’s published over 70 books.

I don’t write genre fiction, but I still keep a copy of King’s bible for authors On Writing near my desk. I pull it out every time I’m procrastinating or unsure what to write about. It’s also a great insight into what it takes to work in a quiet room by yourself for months, 45 years on end.

That book contains lots of gems, including this one, if you ever find yourself writing and rewriting a piece for months.

“Write with the door closed, rewrite with the door open.”

He also offers up this piece of writing advice which is perhaps a mantra for his entire career:

“If you want to be a writer, you must do two things above all others: read a lot and write a lot. There’s no way around these two things that I’m aware of, no shortcut.”

In other words, keep writing and you’ll build up a body of work that you’re happy to publish. Just don’t forget to press publish.

I don’t want you to wait 45 years to hit publish! If you’re having trouble with writer’s block, you’ll enjoy this course.

Write on,

Bryan Collins

title: What's Your Konami Code?
html:
Hi Reader,

Up, up, down, down, left, right, left, right, B, A and start.

Many gamers know that button sequence intimately.

The Konami Code is a famous video game hack.

Japanese video game designer Kazuhisa Hashimoto built this code into his 1986 cult classic Gradius.

His game was too difficult for most people to play, so he created a cheat code.

After pressing these buttons, players received all available power-ups.

Since then, game designers baked the Konami Code into titles like Street Fight II Turbo, League of Legends and Metal Gear Solid.

Gamers (like me) pressed the Konami Code to cheat and get to the next level faster.

I loved Gradius but I don’t play games much these days.

But I discovered I could bake the Konami code in other areas of life, too.

I’d a six-figure gig as an in-house copywriter a few years ago.

I wrote about financial software for small businesses.

The job paid well.

And I worked from home.

But a 50-hour corporate gig wasn’t easy, with the endless product launches, Microsoft Teams calls, and deadlines.

I was also building my writing and self-publishing business on the side.

Now factor in two small kids.

And you’ve got me up every morning at 5 am to write for an hour or two before.

And finishing work every day at 6 or 7 pm.

One afternoon, my work friend asked me, “What happened?”

I didn’t know what she meant.

Then I looked in the mirror.

I looked like I had two black eyes, but not from a crazy Irish bar fight.

I was exhausted.

I knew I couldn’t keep working 80-hour weeks across my two jobs, no matter how lucrative my corporate job was and how I enjoyed building an online writing business.

I needed a Konami code.

So, one morning, instead of opening Scrivener to work on a book draft, I logged onto UpWork.

I set up a job ad for a virtual assistant.

I’m embarrassed to admit it now, but I hired the first applicant.

Thankfully, she worked out.

She helped me publish articles on my website and social media.

Easy to work with, she freed me up to write a book.

After a year, she moved to another line of work.

Now, I faced a new problem.

I knew I couldn’t hire like that again.

And I’d no easy way to hand over all her projects to a new hire.

I found a solution that saved me hours each week.

Since then, I’ve documented every part of my writing business work with team members.

That way, it’s much easier to hand over projects as goals change and hires come and go.

And I can focus on my most important writing project for an hour or two.

(These days, it’s my daily newsletter.)

Outsourcing and creating standard operating procedures is one Konami Code I use to run my writing business with a team of remote employees today.

I’ve a few other Konami codes too.

So why am I telling you all this?

I’ve created a Konami Code for amateur writers who want to turn pro. It’ll help you create more revenue-generating assets for your writing business… in less time.

title: Secrets of 4 Rich Writers
html:
Hi Reader,

How do rich writers do it?

Did they sign a Faustian pact to earn millions while other writers struggle to earn a living?

Here’s what I found out.

1 Don’t worry about rejection - JK Rowling is worth over a billion.

12 different publishers rejected the first Harry Potter book, which she wrote in local coffee shops while broke and in the middle of a painful divorce.

Eventually, a publisher took a chance on her and bought the series for £1.3m.

Even crypto doesn’t produce those returns.

Now, almost anything JK Rowling scribbles on sells (except her X posts and anti-trans rants).

One of her more recent books, a 31-page title measuring 1.6 x 2.4 inches, sold for over $180,000 at an auction.

The lesson here? Send more pitches, DMs, and connection requests.

And stay off X.

2 Keep to a strict publishing schedule - James Patterson is worth at least $800m.

Love or loathe him, Patterson has published over 200 novels and dozens of short stories. Patterson follows a strict formula for his thriller. He finishes between 12–14 books a year.

That’s more than one a month.

Patterson doesn’t spend much time rewriting or revising his drafts. I watched an interview with Patterson where he said he couldn’t care about flowery sentences or immaculate prose. The production line must go on.

He teams up with well-known authors like Maxine Paetro and (even US presidents) so he can tap into their audiences.

But perhaps his biggest secret is working with ghostwriters… and no, not just slapping Bill Clinton’s name on the book cover. He’ll knock out a plot outline and hand it over to a ghost author to write up.

I’m not a huge Patterson fan, but I know about creative output and marketing chops.

When building Become a Writer Today, I hired a team of writers to knock out dozens of weekly articles: my own production line. I also use outlines like Patterson for almost all my content.

3 Set time aside for deep work - Jonathan Franzen is worth at least $5m… I guess literary fiction doesn’t sell as much as genre fiction!

The American novelist behind Freedom and Strong Motion seeks solitude by disconnecting himself from the internet.

During a book tour for his 2012 novel Freedom, Jonathan Franzen told a journalist he wanted to write more daily.

In Franzen’s case, writing more sometimes means flowery sentences that go over an entire page (something that’d give Patterson a heart attack).

So, he turned on hardcore mode.

He physically removed his Wi-Fi card from his computer and permanently blocked his machine’s ethernet connection with Super Glue.

I didn’t destroy my laptop to write, but I sometimes work with Freedom.

(It’s an odd coincidence that this app shares the same name as one of Franzen’s books.)

Freedom cuts me off from the toxic Dopamine feed that is X and the alluring rabbit hole that is Instagram for most of the day.

4 Embrace research - Robert Greene is worth at least $7m.

He’s behind popular self-help books like Mastery and The 48 Laws of Power.

The latter is the second most banned book in US prisons.

Greene’s secret?

Inputs equal outputs.

Greene spends years researching his books. He keeps library index cards full of notes, ideas, and quotes, categorizing and organizing them.

That may explain why his books contain hundreds of primary and secondary sources, quotes, and studies.

Like Patterson, he also taps into other people's audience. He wrote The 50th Law with 50 Cent.

Authors like Greene inspired me to improve my research process. I created a course about how I organize my ideas. It’s called the Zettelkästen Method for writers. You can buy it here.

Write on,
Bryan Collins

title: The procrastination trap: How to avoid it
html:
Hi Reader,

The other day, I spent a morning watching an online writing course by a famous author.

I felt warm and fuzzy about the advice in this course…until later that night.

I realized I’d forgotten to write a daily email for my newsletter.

I was too busy scrubbing through his videos on x2.

Que a scramble to draft and write an email on my Macbook before bed.

I hate writing late at night because staring at my laptop messes up my sleep.

I also find it harder to write when tired.

But I’d only myself to blame.

Spending a morning taking a course instead of writing was a procrastination trap.

Because of some perceived momentum (completing video after video), I felt like I was working.

But in reality?

I was stuck inside a deceptive little trap that was hard to get out of.

Now, don’t get me wrong.

Writing courses are fun (and sometimes useful) but not first thing in the morning.

Completing a course and getting a digital badge won’t help me hit a word count, finish a creative project, or grow my writing business.

Get specific if you find yourself stuck in a procrastination trap like me.

What will you write?

When will you write?

Where will you write?

For how long?

And how will you know when it’s done?

Successful writers either hold themselves accountable or rely on external pressures to avoid the procrastination trap.

Ernest Hemingway famously kept a blackboard next to where he wrote.

Every day, he totalled up his word count and chalked it on the board to not fool himself.

Neil Gaiman forces himself to sit in a writing shed for several hours every day and either write… or do nothing.

I coach a few Pro Writers, and every week, I email them to see if they’re on track.

Now, I don’t use a blackboard like Hemingway.

But I like holding myself accountable with questions like the ones above. I also keep a simple daily checklist.

I’ve four items on my daily checklist for this season.

These items map to the goals for my writing business.

I tick these off on the whiteboard at the end of the working day.

  • Write and send a daily email (you’re reading it!)
  • Post on LinkedIn to grow my email list
  • Make an offer to subscribers
  • Help a client or customer

If I don’t tick these off, I’m either procrastinating or working on the wrong things at the wrong time… like taking a writing course first thing.

But if I tick these items off, I can keep the lights on in my writing business.

Then, I’m free to work on other creative projects, go to the gym, or scrub through a writing course.

Write on,
Bryan Collins

title: I Missed All My Writing Deadlines Until I Did ONE Thing
html:
Hi Reader,

A writer said to me the other day, "I don’t have much time to write, I have a lot going on at work and at home…and I don’t have much time.”

If you’re struggling with this type of problem, consider this advice from NYT journalist David Brooks. He said:

"Great creative minds think like artists but work like accountants.”

Like an accountant preparing a tax return, effective writers use deadlines to finish things.

I worked as a freelance journalist for a few years.

I learned the hard way not to miss deadlines…

After I missed a few deadlines while writing for a local newspaper, I almost got fired.

Later, I lost a profitable magazine writing gig because I submitted my article on Monday morning, hours before it went to press.

Editors don’t care if you’re busy or need more ideas. They want something to publish ON TIME.

If a writer can’t deliver, they’ll hire someone else.

So, I started pushing clients and editors on due dates before agreeing to write the proposed article.

When an editor or a client said, “I need a 1,000-word article about the latest productivity apps.”

or

“Send me an 800-word article about the weird habits of entrepreneurs.”

I’d ask them, “When do you need it for?”

I put the date in Google Calendar.

I also put in a second date, a few days before the actual deadline.

I work towards meeting my imagined deadline. It was kind of like a safety net.

If I got sick or procrastinated, I’d still have a small window to finish the article.

I’d also have an article ready in case an editor or client came to me looking for something at the last minute to commission.

I don’t write for newspapers, Irish magazines, or truculent editors anymore. However, I still set myself real and imagined deadlines for my writing business.

Here are two examples:

  • Write and publish a daily newsletter every morning
  • Write and publish one post on LinkedIn every afternoon

Setting deadlines forces me to avoid anything distracting, like wasting time on X or Insta. I also keep track of the deadlines I hit and miss each week, real and imagined.

So, if you’re struggling with deadlines, put two dates into your personal content calendar. The first real one is from a client, editor, boss, or for an important creative project.

Now set a second imagined one, a few days earlier to allow. It’s your buffer for “The dog ate my homework” contingencies.

Remember, readers will turn up if you publish consistently, and clients are more likely to hire you again if you submit on time.

You don’t need more time or better ideas.

You just need to press submit or publish.

Setting two deadlines is one of the concepts I teach freelance writers. If you need help holding yourself freelancing, check out my course Freelance Writing Mastery.

Write on,
Bryan Collins

title: Can a club help you write?
html:
Hi Reader,

I've joined many clubs over the years.

Some I quit almost immediately.

Others I stayed in for years.

Some examples?

Toastmasters to practice public speaking.

A weightlifting club in a local CrossFit gym to put on some muscle.

An athletics club to learn how to run.

And a Star Trek appreciation club because I was a spotty-faced teenager.

One club left a big impression on me.

Years ago, I joined Write Club.

Write Club was a local creative writing group.

(Not the most original name, granted).

A dozen of us met each month in a bar in Dublin every Monday night.

We drank pitchers of beer, riffed about the craft, and shared reading recommendations about Irish authors like Clare Keegan and John Banville.

At the time I was struggling to pay the bills, and I relished this social support network for aspiring Irish writers.

But the real benefit of Write Club?

Accountability.

You see, each week, we critiqued each other’s pieces.

Fiction.

Non-fiction.

Short stories.

Personal essays

You name it.

I knew I couldn’t turn up on Monday evenings with a blank page and an excuse about work being busy.

So, I forced myself to write something every week.

My somethings were terrible.

But they were also the fermentation of a lasting writing habit.

Even though I stopped writing genre fiction, that writing habit helped me write online and build my business.

Alas, Write Club has long since disbanded.

We went our separate ways to find jobs, have babies, and embrace receding hairlines (me).

The other day, I Googled a few past members.

I was pleasantly surprised to find one is a successful genre fiction author.

A few others write non-fiction for their jobs.

(Think books, journalism, and academia).

I sometimes miss the comradeship of connecting with other writers.

So, I’m launching an affordable community for writers who want to write online, connect with each other, and build a business around the craft.

I’d like to avoid a Reddit free-for-all of trolls and bots.

title: What my writing routine looks like
html:
Hi Reader,

I quit my day job to work on my writing business in 2020.

These days, I work in a home office.

I get up around 7 AM and drop the kids off at school. Then, I drink coffee and read some non-fiction on my Kindle.

I also use a meditation app called The Way for 10–20 minutes.

Around 9 AM, I put on a pair of noise-canceling headphones and play ambient music on Spotify. I then open an app called Flow and set a timer for 90 minutes.

I work on my main creative project for the day.

Some current examples include writing this daily newsletter and YouTube scripts. I’ll also outline ideas for future projects, such as a book.

If I’m stuck for ideas, I’ll journal and write down ideas from books I’ve read.

Sometimes, I track my word count, but 90 minutes is more than enough to make meaningful progress, whether I’m editing or writing.

(Years ago, I worked in blocks of 30 minutes. But I get much more done if I can sit in the chair and focus for 90 minutes).

After 90 minutes, I take a half-hour break to eat breakfast and brew tea.

I used to eat porridge and scrub through online courses on x2 over breakfast. But cramming more content into my head first thing fries my brain.

Then, I’ll work for another 90 minutes.

I set hard rules about social media in the morning. I’ve disabled all the platforms on my Mac using an app called Freedom. I also removed them from my iPhone.

In the afternoon, I don’t write. I usually work in a gym near our house or go for a run near a local canal.

After that, I take calls, post on LinkedIn, and work with a few clients. I’ll also ensure the trains run on time by checking invoicing or fixing technical problems with my site, and finally, I use social media.

Then, I collect the kids from school.

And after dinner…

I’m in the middle of training for a triathlon, so I’ll also get in a second workout, such as a swim or a cycle.

Or I’ll connect with other writers and creators I know who run similar online businesses.

At night, I write my priorities for the following day on a whiteboard in my office. I based these priorities on my daily checklist. Basically, I need to do 4–5 things every day.

Here are some examples:

  • Writing and sending a daily email
  • Posting on LinkedIn to grow my newsletter
  • Making an offer to a potential client
  • Working with a client or student

The point here isn’t that you should reverse engineer my writing routine…or anyone else’s.

I can focus for 90 minutes because I’m working on my business full-time. I don’t have to stop to take calls or attend a Zoom meeting.

I’d have found that impossible when working as a copywriter in my corporate life.

Writing full-time can be an isolating experience. I struggle with this problem too. Writers regularly tell me they’d love to connect with other writers.

title: The Loneliness Trap: How You Can Avoid It
html:
Hi Reader,

I smoked 15 cigarettes a day for a few years.

You see…

At the time, I was writing by myself in the mornings and late at night.

I wasn’t making much progress either.

I didn’t know how to hold myself accountable.

I wrote and rewrote the same pieces for weeks on end.

I had no idea about how to build an audience.

I didn’t know anyone who could help me with these problems.

And worst of all, I wasn’t getting paid despite spending hours at my desk.

The experience was miserable, frustrating and lonely.

(A study in PLOS Medicine says feeling this way is as bad for your health as smoking up to 15 cigarettes.)

Here’s how I kicked my bad habit:

First up, I joined a non-fiction writing group in Dublin.

We met up once a week to talk about the craft.

And thanks to critiques from a cranky writing instructor from Texas, I figured out how to write non-fiction.

I also built a network of other writers I could talk to about creative problems like writer’s block.

Of course, they couldn’t help me get paid or build a business around writing.

So, I joined an online marketing group.

There, I discovered how to build an audience.

I honed my online writing chops.

And I figured out that full-time writers work as hard on their business as on their craft.

Now, writing today is still a solitary profession.

Writers spend hours working alone in a spare room, a coffee shop, or a library daily.

They must also contend with the latest tech like ChatGPT and shifting social media algos.

But that doesn’t mean writing part-time or full-time needs to feel lonely.

Wanting to write shouldn’t damage your health, like smoking 15 cigarettes a day.

That’s where a community of like-minded peers can help.

You can get feedback from other peers.

You can ask beginner and advanced questions about topics like books, writing online and building a writing business.

You can also share wins.

And you can find other creatives who can hold you accountable.

title: Hemingway's Lost Suitcase
html:
Hi Reader,

Ernest Hemingway lost all of his best ideas.

In 1922, a young Hemingway was on assignment in Switzerland.

He was a foreign correspondent for the Toronto Star newspaper.

Meanwhile, his wife Hadley, traveling from Paris to see him, packed up Hemingway's papers, writing and manuscripts into a suitcase.

Hadley was a thorough suitcase packer. She'd even included the carbons - 1922 speaks for iCloud backups ;)

While the train was waiting in the Gare de Lyon, Hadley went outside to buy a bottle of Evian water. She returned to her seat to find the suitcase ROBBED.

Hemingway's drafts, stories, and novel manuscripts–ones he'd spent years working on…

Gone!

Ernest had nothing left except for a poem and two short stories, one buried in a drawer and the other with an editor.

(I don't know about you, but I get frustrated when iCloud or Google Docs messes up version control or some of my articles don't sync.)

Hemingway was about to land a writing contract for his fiction.

He was under pressure to show something to his editor.

So, he started again.

He wrote during the day as a journalist to pay the bills.

At night, he worked from memory, rewriting his stories.

He kept a large blackboard next to where he worked.

He wrote down his daily word count each day to hold himself accountable.

While rewriting his stories, Hemingway cut flowery sentences.

He rewrote his stories using concise, everyday words.

He stripped the "language clean, to lay it bare down to the bone."

Thanks to a suitcase thief, he embraced a minimalistic form of writing, which he later became famous for.

The missing suitcase also taught Hemingway that his subconscious could work on stories even if he didn't have his draft and notes to hand.

He later said:

The most important thing I've learned about writing is never write too much at a time… Never pump yourself dry. Leave a little for the next day. The main thing is to know when to stop. Don't wait till you've written yourself out. When you're still going good and you come to an interesting place and you know what's going to happen next, that's the time to stop. Then leave it alone and don't think about it; let your subconscious mind do the work.

Hemingway's Lost Suitcase illustrates the power of a creative constraint.

You don't always need more time.

You don't always need more ideas.

You don't always need more research.

Remember, your subconscious is working on your stories and drafts even when you're doing something else.

So, turn up even if you feel like progress is slow.

Ask yourself these questions:

"How can I get the same or better results with less money or time?"

"What can I take out, cut, or stop doing to go from the first draft to DONE?"

The answers will help you impose a creative constraint.

Like giving yourself a deadline, real or imagined.

Or forcing yourself to rewrite an entire piece in one session.

Or, finally, publishing a piece you've spent months procrastinating about.

Using creative constraints is one of the principles I teach in my Conquer Writer's Block course. Check it out.

Write on,
Bryan Collins

title: I don't know what my niche is
html:
Hi Reader,

Lots of writers worry about niche selection.

Should they try to become the productivity guy?

Or the Notion template girl?

I tumbled down this rabbit hole for a few years.

At the time, I was a Forbes columnist.

So, I picked the topic of “productivity and time management.”

A classic business niche.

One smack bang in the middle of the Forbes wheelhouse.

(Or at least it was before they started publishing mattress reviews and cat info articles.)

I spent an hour researching hot articles and topics about getting things done at work each week.

I mapped dozens of hot topics from the world of productivity in a Google Sheet. Then, I’d pick one to write each day.

I published articles like:

  • The Fastest Way To Accomplish More This Week
  • How To Use The 4 Ds Of Effective Time Management
  • 5 Characteristics Of Successful, Productive Entrepreneurs
  • 5 Simple Ways Elon Musk Accomplishes The Impossible

I published some duds.

And a few viral hits.

I liken this approach to writing from the top down.

Mapping content to cover is great for businesses in need of a strategy.

They can only afford to invest time and resources in content that helps them sell their product or service.

I still use this approach when consulting.

But for my work?

I write from the bottom up.

I don’t care about covering every topic related to productivity, creativity, writing, freelancing, copywriting, getting paid to write, chasing vanity metrics, fancy Notion templates, why I loathe 99% of AI writing apps…

I enjoy reading about all of these topics, but I don’t have a list of articles I need to publish this month.

I’m not publishing content to appease some pseudo-CMO of my writing business who will fire me if I don’t hit a traffic or revenue goal.

Instead, I capture notes from interesting articles, podcasts, videos, and books.

I take note of things I’m working on.

I write about problems in my writing business.

I snag ideas from other people’s creative businesses.

I review my notes once a week to see if I can spot any odd connections. I also look for emerging themes.

Then, I pick a theme and write about it for my newsletter. Or I can turn it into a LinkedIn post.

If that content resonates, I’ll turn it into long-form content like an article or a video.

This way, I can experiment with different topics without worrying about deep voice niche selection. I can get feedback from individual pieces of content. And I can reach different readers.

I prefer this approach because I can become a niche simply by what I write and publish.

Any creative can.

Classic writing advice says: “Think of a friend… and write to them.”

The thing is…

When talking to a friend, you don’t announce, “I want to tell you about all things time management, getting sh*t done at work or Notion.”

Instead, you chat with your friend about what’s on your mind and what’s interesting about it.

Good writing isn’t any different.

So why am I telling you this?

Writing from the bottom up is one of the principles I teach in my course, The Zettelkästen Method for Writers. It’s open today.

Write on,
Bryan Collins

title: Surgeon general wants social media warning labels
html:
Hi Reader,

The US Surgeon General wants to slap red warning labels on Facebook, Insta, TikTok, and X.

Warnings like the ones you’ll read on packets of cigarettes, fatty foods, and bottles of booze.

Dr Vivek Murthy says TikTok-like platforms are causing a mental health crisis for young people.

(Who would have guessed all that doom scrolling was toxic?!)

Teenagers spend not one but FOUR hours a day madly swiping, scrolling, sharing, and liking.

It’s the same depressing story in Ireland.

The chief bottle washers here are pontificating about banning social media for those under 13.

They’re making guttural noises about bringing in a digital age of consent.

I’ve no idea how they’ll enforce anything like that.

I tried it.

I brought in a social media ban in our house.

No iPad for our youngest before school.

Screentime restrictions at night-time, too.

I used apps like Freedom to whisk the internet away first thing and late at night.

The kids weren’t happy.

Neither was I!

One of them found a way around my internet restrictions…

I also brought in some rules for me too.

You see…

A few months ago, I launched a new project: write daily on social media.

I wanted to grow my writing business with some juicy organic social traffic.

(If I’m honest, I wanted to go viral.)

I researched what other creators write about on X, LinkedIn, Insta, and Threads.

I decided to write on all these platforms as well.

I studied the top hooks, formats, headlines, and content types.

I interviewed a few top creators in my niche.

And I got to work.

But…

Chasing likes, shares, and views across multiple platforms burnt me out within weeks.

I spent more time eating out on other people’s content than writing my own.

Some of my content popped, but the experience still left me sick about my stats and engagement.

I felt like I’d shoveled McDonald’s down my gullet three times a day for weeks.

All that fatty social media content gave me a classic case of social media comparisonitis.

The cure?

A realization that I can’t eat out on likes, shares, and views alone.

All those vanity metrics won’t fuel a writing business.

Try it, and your cash flow will quickly dry up.

Sure, some social platforms will pay you to create content for them.

(I’ve earned some nice payouts from platforms like Medium over the years.)

But, payouts from partner programs are crumbs from the table.

Most creators on these platforms are underpaid.

These platforms tip their sudo-employees to work for them.

They keep the real wedge for themselves.

By all means, write on social.

But get those followers onto your email list.

Then, build your writing business.

I’m still working on a project: write for social media.

But I’ve slapped a red warning label across the tin.

Leave going viral to the Mr Beast's of this world.

Instead…

Create a product, a service or an offer that builds a business.

title: You're working too hard
html:
Hi Reader,

Did you hear the one about Parkinson’s Law?

Here’s how it works:

Work expands to fill all the time available.

Give yourself a day to write a 1,000-word article at 10 cents per word, and it will take 24 hours.

I let you work on the math on what that means for your rate per hour…

Give yourself a month for a writing project, and you’ll be swearing at Microsoft Word on the 31st.

Give yourself three months to write a book, and getting to The END will take four.

(If you’re anything like me, that last one will take at least six.)

Anyway, I’m a productivity nerd.

So, here’s how I use Parkinson’s Law for my writing projects.

I focus on the 20% of activities moving my business forward.

(Hint: for most writers and business owners, that 20% is writing emails and newsletters.)

I outsource, delay, or DON’T DO the rest.

I get high-strike projects on my To-do list.

Here’s a fun list of things I stopped over the past few months:

  • Recording short-form reels for Insta even though an overpriced social media guru said it’d grow my account faster
  • Writing mega X threads and posts because the reach and politics suck
  • Repurposing content on TikTok… because it rots my brain
  • Recording a weekly podcast because I did it for five years, and sometimes projects end

I could go on, but we’re both busy.

I’ve more emails to write.

You’ve more clients to get.

So, here’s the 20% of the email that will get you the most results.

Give yourself a deadline to finish that 20%… today.

You don’t need to craft immaculate emails, LinkedIn or X posts.

(You don’t need X… at all)

Instead, hit publish early and often.

Then, make more offers.

Remember…

You don’t need more likes and followers.

You need readers, clients, and customers.

Get paid to create.

Don’t create to get paid.

If that sounds like your bag, I can help. I’ve 2 spots open in Pro Writers Only. Reply to this email to learn more.

Bryan Collins

title: Wells Fargo wants to fire you
html:
Hi Reader,

So Wells Fargo fired a bunch of bank workers a few days ago.

Get this.

They were pretending to work at their desks.

They used some odd tech to fake keyboard typing instead of doing their “actual jobs.”

A whole industry of software and tools exists to fake keyboard presses and mouse movements.

Perhaps I should fire myself from my writing business.

I pretend to work all the time.

This past Monday morning, I dropped my son off at school on his bike…

I walked home and brewed a coffee…

I turned on my Mac…

I set a timer for 90 minutes…

I opened up my writing app…

And I pressed random buttons on my keyboard until the buzzer went off…

(That messy draft read like I’d pressed buttons)

And another afternoon…

I finished reading The Adweek Copywriting Handbook.

I put the book down and stared into space, thinking about a copywriting project when my teenage daughter marched in from school.

“What are you doing?!”

“Working!” I said

“You’re so odd.”

I blame Neil Gaiman.

He says he regularly trots out to his writing shed.

Gaiman’s shed doesn’t have the internet, distractions, or AI.

(He keeps a lot of fancy fountain pens, though. Gaiman prefers pens to digital tools)

Now, at his writing desk…

Gaiman can do one of two things: nothing or write.

Here’s the thing with nothing:

Sometimes, nothing is something.

And something is enough.

Writing doesn’t always happen at your desk or at the end of a target word count.

It’s not always something you can quantify, track, or report to your line manager at the bank.

Those random sentences and paragraphs?

They’re the makings of a first draft.

And that first draft can turn into something you can publish… if you keep turning up to work on it.

Reading a copywriting book and using ONE idea for your current project or writing business?

That’s work too…

No matter how odd or lazy it looks.

title: Don’t rely on partner programs to get paid
html:
Hi Reader,

I’ve earned thousands of dollars from partner programs like Medium.

I wrote viral articles, and they paid me several hundred dollars each month.

And now some content creators I know are getting paid to create content for Facebook and Instagram.

Sure, it’s nice when a social media network pays YOU to create content for THEM.

In reality?

You’re a slave to an algo that can change at any time…

You’re leaving money on the table…

And you’re working for less than you think…

As an example…

The other day, I divided what Medium paid me by the words published.

The rate came in at far less than 10 cents.

(And now the Medium algo is making it MUCH harder for writers over there to earn a decent living.)

The reality?

Many easier strategies exist for getting paid to write.

I recommend these strategies to Pro Writers.

One example?

Finding clients.

I love working with clients who take building a writing business seriously.

It’s more rewarding because…

  1. You can help someone else
  2. It pays more than producing dozens of articles
  3. You learn more about your audience

Now client work isn’t for everyone.

I get that.

But you can also productize yourself and what you know into a type of digital product.

Then you can sell increasing levels of access.

That way, you can increase your income… and spend more time writing.

title: It’s Ok to Charge More
html:
Hi Reader,

Usually, writers and creators start with low-ticket offers.

These exist at the bottom of an offer pyramid.

That’s what I did a few years ago, and it’s a mistake.

Here’s why:

I started by selling books.

Books are fun to write, but they take months to ship, and they don’t generate a great return.

Other writers follow a similar approach with printables and low-price digital downloads.

You’ve got to sell a lot of these to earn.

I also scraped together money from the Medium partner program and freelancing.

Freelancing is time-intensive.

Partner programs are a grind.

Lucrative, yes, but affiliates regularly change and even kill their programs.

Courses are profitable, but students don’t always take them.

title: 100s of writers fired because of AI
html:
Hi Reader,

I read a BBC article the other day about a troubled content agency. They let over 60 writers go… and replaced them with AI.

The agency wanted to cut costs.

And that’s only one of many stories about writers losing work because of robots.

Since 2020, I have spent thousands of dollars commissioning work from content agencies. These agencies employ writers who produce content for website owners and small businesses.

Here’s how the content model worked:

Website owners like me research an article, draft an outline, identify the keywords, and prepare a brief.

Then, we order a batch of these articles from an agency for an agreed word count, usually 6–10 cents per word.

The agency turns around a draft in 2–3 days. We go through one round of revisions and click publish.

If the website owner likes the content, they stick with an agency or a group of writers and order articles every week.

(A variation of this model applies to hiring writers and producing content in-house.)

But not anymore…

I know of at least three agencies that went into administration or closed over the past 12 months.

The owners ALL claim AI killed their bottom line.

You see…

Some business owners are using AI in place of human writers. They’re using tools like ChatGPT to produce content for a fraction of the cost.

One business owner even confessed to me that he fired his marketing team.

“AI can do a better job,” he said.

Relying on AI strikes me as misguided…

Hundreds of websites have lost the bulk of their traffic and revenue thanks to a brutal series of Google algorithm updates.

You see…

Google doesn’t like AI content appearing in search results… unless it’s from its own AI tool, Gemini.

I don’t care much about mass-producing and publishing lousy AI content, so I quit publishing content at scale.

But reading about writers losing their jobs because of AI hurts me.

I was a freelance writer years ago, too.

As a freelancer who has spent hours looking for work and as a publisher who spent $1000s hiring…

I’ve a feeling that those businesses publishing bland, boring AI content are sacrificing quality for speed.

Even if they’re not dependent on Google search traffic, they’re investing time in bargain-basement content.

But that doesn’t change the fact that AI isn’t going anywhere.

Writers must adapt.

I get pitches most days from writers who want me to hire them.

They promise an “error-free, SEO optimized” article.

One guy even said, “Can you do me a solid? I need the work!”

He shared a Google folder with his portfolio.

The days of working as a generic content writer are numbered.

An ability to research and write an article and charge 6–10 cents per word isn’t enough.

And neither is a folder stuffed full of generic articles.

Business owners don’t care that said content is error-free, factual, and SEO-optimized.

They can get a version of that from our AI overlords.

And they’re not about to commission a writer because they feel sorry for them.

So, what is a struggling writer supposed to do these days?

Think beyond generic content and word counts.

ChatGPT can do that.

Some content writers are finding work editing AI content. They edit and fact-check generated content to ensure it passes AI detection tests.

Even that strikes me as a gap that AI will rapidly close.

What businesses need is a content strategy.

Can you help a business owner identify what types of content to publish, where, and when?

Can you help them craft an educational email course or a high-converting lead magnet?

Instead of positioning yourself as a content writer, provide a service to a select group of clients.

It’s much harder for AI to provide a personalized service to business owners. You can charge more, too.

If you want to increase your income as a writer, join my workshop next week.

You can buy a ticket below.

Write on,

Bryan Collins

title: Fun side hustles for writers
html:
Hi Reader,

I didn’t quit my job to write full-time until I had turned not one but two side hustles into reliable income streams.

My first side hustle?

Freelancing.

I freelanced as a copywriter for Irish businesses and websites.

Some months I’d earn more than my full-time job.

Other months, I didn’t earn much.

I knew I couldn’t rely on a yo-yo income from freelancing writing alone.

(That said, Writers Work makes it easier to land freelance jobs today.)

So, I also started a second side hustle.

Writing and self-publishing books on Amazon.

I spent hundreds of hours writing, self-publishing and promoting my books.

Looking back, that wasn’t the easiest or best side hustle to start. But I don’t regret it.

Writing books is a great credibility builder.

It helped me grow an audience.

And it’s fun.

If you want to write on the side, here are 3 more fun side hustles for writers.

You can easily earn a few K a month from any of these.

And they don’t require working 40, 50 and 60 hour weeks, either.

1 Start a paid newsletter

It’s easier than ever to launch a paid newsletter.

All you need?

A good topic.

An ideal reader.

A willingness to write and publish short daily emails.

Beehiiv, Substack and ConvertKit all enable paid newsletters and landing sponsors.

2 Offer coaching and consulting

Coaching and consulting are good side hustles. You likely have some experiences and ideas that you take for granted.

Turn those experiences into content.

Publish that content on LinkedIn… or where your ideal client spends their time.

Then, explain how connections can work with you to achieve the same results.

3 Ghostwriting

Chances are you take expressing yourself through the written word for granted.

To others, that skill is either a mystery or something that takes them waaaaay too long to learn.

Business owners will gladly pay you to write and create content on their behalf.

All you have to do is pitch.

title: How I get paid to write
html:
Hi Reader,

I was a broke writer in my twenties.

I was too busy playing video games and trying to write THE BOOK… instead of figuring out how to build a writing business.

In my 30s, I landed a job as an in-house copywriter.

I picked up skills I still use today to write online.

Now, as your internet elder (I’m 42!), I work on my writing business full-time.

Well ALMOST.

Someday I take the afternoon off to pick the kids up from school or go for a long run.

Perhaps you’re at a different stage?

I want to explain what did and didn’t work, so you can build a writing business too.

You see…

I’ve tried dozens of different strategies for getting paid to write online.

I spent thousands taking courses and dozens of hours talking to experts about all of these strategies.

Some were massive successes (like +6 figures).

Others were a TOTAL crash and burn.

Some STILL work today.

Others, less so.

Here are just a few of the strategies I tried:

Writing and self-publishing books on Kindle - Fun, but not directly profitable.

Creating digital downloads like printables - Crash and burn. Requires massive volume.

Freelance writing - Time-consuming. Revenue was sporadic, too.

Copywriting - Lucrative. Every writer should know the basics.

Building content websites - Was very profitable. Less so today.

Coaching and consulting - A sweet spot for many writers who want to go pro.

Creating online courses - Profitable if you have an email list, but not as easy as hustle X says.

Writing for social media partner programs - Fun, but don’t get sucked into thinking this is a good job.

I’ll walk through all of these strategies in detail, sharing what worked, what didn’t work, and what strategy I’d employ today.

title: I built niche websites for years
html:
Hi Reader,

I quit building niche websites.

I recommended this business model to other writers.

I was even offered 6 figures for one site.

And 7 figures for another.

Building niche websites WAS a great model for writers and bloggers.

Not anymore.

  2. AI is lowering the barrier to entry
  3. Google hates content websites
  4. Search engines are using your content for free
  5. Social media platforms are using AI too

I’ve abandoned most of my content websites.

I picked a different business model.

So what am I doing now?

I’m doubling down on my newsletter.

I’m doubling down on coaching, copywriting and client work.

I’m writing what AI can’t.

title: I spent over $32,427 on online writing courses
html:
Hi Reader,

I’m a writing course junkie.

Years ago, I paid for creative writing classes at the Irish Writers Center in Dublin.

Since then, I’ve paid for online writing courses about copywriting, SEO, blogging and the craft.

Here’s what I found out.

Document what you learn.

Taking a writing course and doing nothing with it is procrastination in disguise.

Writing up your learnings as blog posts, articles or social media posts can pay dividends in unusual ways.

I took several business writing courses to upskill for a new corporate job back in 2015.

I paid for them on LinkedIn Learning. Back then, it was called Lynda.

I wrote about the course on a personal blog.

One day, a friend at work said he stumbled across my review. I checked my web stats and was surprised to see thousands of people read my review each month.

The LinkedIn Learning team invited me into their affiliate program, and I quickly earned $1000. That paid for the course… and then some.

Reframe premium writing courses as an investment

It’s a big decision, whipping out your credit card and paying a couple of $ for a course.

The first premium course I bought was from Jon Morrow. His course cost $2000. That was a lot of money to pay for a course from some random guy I’d met on Twitter.

I typed in my credit card details, thinking, “I can’t afford this!"

But… the course helped me learn how to write online and sell digital products.

I met Jon a few years later in Austin, Texas, as part of his mastermind and worked with several of his clients.

Use what works, discard the rest

I try to apply one or two strategies from a writing course I like.

As an example, I used an odd writing strategy David Sedaris teaches in his Masterclass.

(Sedaris recommends writing a daily journal like a scene from a novel and then using the results for non-fiction.)

However, I don’t expect a writing course to always deliver the goods… no matter how accomplished the teacher is.

For example, technical writing courses date… fast.

Many of the SEO courses I’ve paid for are out-of-date post ChatGPT or flat-out wrong.

I all but ignore the SEO writing gurus, no matter what they’re flogging these days.

Pick a writing course to solve one problem

A good course focuses on a specific problem and helps students solve it. I took a YouTube course from Pat Flynn.

His course is concise and focuses on starting a YouTube channel. I used his course to improve my YouTube scripts.

Community beats any lesson

The online course market is saturated. People don’t need another few hours of video to scrub through on x2.

And some writing courses from online gurus are nothing more than upsells for an overpriced premium offer.

But…

Buying a writing course is great for forming connections with other students.

You can connect with people at or on a level above you and collaborate on creative or business writing projects.

That’s more valuable than half a dozen hours of video.

Some students from courses I’ve taken started their own writing businesses. I worked with a few of them on several profitable projects over the years.

title: EXPERT: Website writing a waste of time?
html:
Hi Reader,

I got on Zoom with a content marketing agency owner the other day.

He asked me about starting a newsletter business.

And I asked him about the reality of running a content marketing agency.

An exchange of ideas.

“I could have expletives on the homepage and nobody would notice,” he said about his agency website. “It’s all but useless for finding clients”

Instead, this agency owner sources most of his clients from word-of-mouth referrals and pitches. His website is a form of social proof, nothing more.

This agency owner is busy publishing content on LinkedIn and building an email list. He takes that more seriously. An expletive in either of those places would stand out.

And another agency owner in Ireland told me his website drives 0 business. “I don’t spend much time working on it,” he said. “Clients don’t find us from search.”

Instead, this agency owner sources clients from his network.

So are websites a waste of time today?

I spent years building and writing on content websites and blogs.

Writing on a personal website or blog is a harder game to play than back in 2020 or even 2016. Standing out in search is hard.

Most readers’ attention spans are frazzled.

They’re too busy swiping madly on their social media app of choice than searching for a random article on a content website.

And that’s before factoring in how AI has lowered the bar for what qualifies as content.

Even then, you’re lucky if a reader spends more than 60 seconds scanning an article that took hours to write (or a few minutes to generate).

And yet…

A big difference exists between agency owners and online writers.

An agency owner gets paid to deliver content for another business. They don’t have to write this content themselves.

Meanwhile, a writer publishes online, usually under their byline.

They enjoy the act of filling a screen with words.

They get a kick out of pressing publish.

To get paid to write today, and you can do both…

Find your ideal client.

(They’re probably on LinkedIn).

Pitch them your writing services.

Then, get paid to create content for them.

And…

Write authentic, personal content that you enjoy… the type that AI can never generate.

Publish it on your personal website.

But treat that site like a newsletter.

(That’s easy with ConvertKit and Substack.)

Using this approach, you can capture the email addresses of readers.

Every time you press publish, they get your latest articles… right in their inbox.

If your work lands in their inbox, readers are far more likely to consume it.

Then, to get paid, make regular offers for your books, courses, and services.

If you need help, my friend Cary is launching Write Publish Profit 7.0 this week. The mega bundle contains over $4,000 of resources for writers who want to earn a good living… including building your email list and selling more books. You can even find a course from yours truly inside. It's all available for just $97 for a limited time.

Check it out

Write on,
Bryan Collins

title: How I Got My First 100 Email Subscribers
html:
Hi Reader,

Carlos wrote in a few days ago. He’s thinking of writing a newsletter. Smart move.

He asked me, “I have no email list other than things I signed up for. What should I do?“

I started my email list years ago on MailChimp. I picked MailChimp because it was free. I didn’t have any money for software, let alone ads or a plan for growing my newsletter.

So, I messaged a few friends and said, “Hey, I’ve started this new blog. Could you join my email list?”

I sent them a link to the opt-in page, and they opted in.

It doesn’t cost me anything.

A few friends opted in. Now, the subscribers weren’t writers, and I wasn’t trying to sell them a product or a service.

These early subscribers were like the well-meaning friend who popped into another friend’s new coffee shop. They’ll buy three coffees and a croissant even though they hate caffeine.

In the early days, I needed that support.

Seeing “Total subscriber count” change from 0 to 10 gave me a small audience to write to.

It gave me an ideal reader... at least in my mind.

Now, I was writing to someone and not into the void.

Over the years, I grew my list to 1,000 and then 10,000 subscribers. I did it via SEO, ads, guest blogging, lead magnets, and a dozen other online marketing strategies (some of which still work today).

As my email list grew, I switched to ConvertKit. By now, I was earning a nice side income from my email list. But, I was also spending more money on a higher-tier ConvertKit plan.

More money. More problems.

You see...

Subscribers sometimes opt-in with fake email addresses to get the free lead magnet.

So, I used ConvertKit to find cold subscribers who hadn't opened my emails over the past few months. I sent them a re-engagement campaign asking them if they still wanted to read my newsletter. Some said yes.

I removed hundreds of cold subscribers who didn’t engage or say they still wanted in.

One day, I met a friend for a pint in a pub near where I live outside Dublin. The same friend who opted in when I started my newsletter.

He asked how my writing business was doing.

Then, he said, “Hey! I don’t get emails from you anymore. Did you stop your newsletter?”

I thought something was wrong with the deliverability of my emails. You see, I was sending weekly emails at this point.

The next morning, I logged into ConvertKit and checked my stats. I found his email address greyed out.

When I’d cleaned my list, I’d removed his address because he hadn’t opened any emails over the past three months or engaged with my newsletter.

I felt guilty about purging an early supporter.

But then I realized I didn’t need the crutch of a friend or family member.

I’d grown an audience of ideal readers.

Many of these readers went on to buy my books.

Books I wrote and self-published.

You can do the same. My friend Cary explains more in his new short ebook Dream Big. Read it here.

Write on,

Bryan Collins

title: Is Google Trying to 🔥 Blogging
html:
Hi Reader,

I was wading through the Google algo leak the other day.

Like many bloggers and content publishers, my traffic is down big-time.

I wanted answers.

I found this gem.

The search algo is ranking blogs and content websites based on click-through rates.

In other words...

If more readers click through to a website and on its content, Google will send more traffic to the site or blog.

Sounds sensible... in theory.

Then, I waded into the search results and found them stuffed with unhelpful AI overviews, random cat articles, air purifier and mattress reviews from Google's friends at Forbes and Reddit.

The problem of lousy AI content even got picked up by the BBC, which described the problem as “an extinction-level event” for content businesses.

Content businesses laying off writers and editors as a result.

How can a content publisher or blogger get more clicks if they don't appear in search in the first place?

Travel writer Katie Caf Travel asked GoogleSearchLiason about this clickthrough issue on X.

Should she publish articles that Google will rank or focus on off-site efforts, i.e., getting social media traffic?

The GoogleSearchLiason X account said content creators should "focus on doing whatever they think is best for their readers."

At first...

That struck me as nothing more than a Kevin Costner Field of Dreams answer:

If you publish great content, they will come.

Building a content business on hopes and dreams isn't a strategy.

But the X account described what great content sites look like today.

"Great sites with content that people like receive traffic in many ways. People go to them directly. They come via email referrals. They arrive via links from other sites. They get social media mentions."

And then the X account laid a more sensible content strategy :

So, if you're starting a writing or content business, invest in multiple traffic sources.

The word email perked my attention.

I've been following a few content publishers who are killing with Facebook and Pinterest traffic. The advertising RPMs from Pinterest are glorious.

I’ve also invested time and energy in sourcing traffic from our social media overlords.

But that's still traffic that our social media overlords can turn on or off like a tap... or even replace with AI content.

(Both Facebook and Pinterest are experimenting with AI content generators.)

Relying on search traffic for a blog or content website is a fool’s errand today.

By all means, play the social media game and the search game.

I intend to.

But consider this:

What do most people look at every morning before work?

Email.

What do most people check on their lunch break?

Email.

And what do most people read at the end of the day?

Email.

It’s the best way to write to readers and present your offers… without worrying about AI or some algorithm change.

Email is also the best method for selling books and growing your writing business. Google can never take that away from you.

On that last point, my friend Cary Richards writes about how to dream big with your writing business in his new book Beyond the Page.

You can download it here.

Write on,

Bryan Collins

title: Elon Musk wants to ban iPhones
html:
Hi Reader,

Musk is putting the kibosh on Apple devices at Tesla and X.

He's telling employees on their way in the door to dump their iOS devices in a Faraday cage.

Musk blames AI.

You see...

A few days ago, the boffins in Cupertino announced Apple Intelligence.

According to Apple mumbo-jumbo, users can now use Apple Intelligence Writing Tools to write, proofread, and "generate content".

To do all this, Siri is passing off some queries to OpenAI.

I roar at my iPhone, and Siri shouts back with a ChatGPT souped-up response.

(Assuming Siri can now finally understand an Irish accent.)

Or I tap madly in Apple Note, and Siri solves my frazzled short-term memory by categorizing and organizing my ideas.

But Musk doesn't like the idea of Siri climbing into bed with OpenAI.

He says, in a deep CEO voice, that it's an "unacceptable security violation."

And this is from the man who let an army of bots and trolls loose on his personal social media platform.

The guy who's building Grok, X's lousy AI tool that summarizes news content and trolls.

I cry a little every time I open X...

But Musk is a smart dude.

The man is building electric Cybertrucks.

He’s also sending rockets to Mars.

So, I'm banning iPhones in my writing business too.

Generating content with AI is an unacceptable violation of my own content standards.

I like using AI to automate boring tasks, like transcribing videos or firing boilerplate responses to spammy outreach emails and off-the-wall pitches.

Not generating boring, bland, vanilla AI-generated content because it's quick and easy...

But relying on AI to add "humor and creativity" (yes, these words are in the Apple press release)...

That's a user experience I'm happy to skip.

Speaking of creativity…

Did you know indie authors published some 2.1 million books since 2021?

I found that stat inside my friend Cary Richards's new ebook. He wants you to dream big with your writing business. Download his book Beyond the Page here.

Write on,

Bryan Collins

title: You're being plagiarised
html:
Hi Reader,

Google’s AI overviews stink.

Its generative AI tool tool is crawling websites of all sizes.

Then, it’s summarizing what it finds, plonking the results on page zero without permission, or investigating if the output is true.

The result?

A bizarre set of search results.

One AI overview suggested putting nontoxic glue in your pizza.

Another suggested the key to staying healthy is eating three rocks a day.

And another said parrots can do a variety of jobs, including working as toy makers, prison inmates, and engineers.

Google’s AI doesn’t always get it wrong.

And it will improve.

In many cases, it nicely summarizes what it finds.

Google CEO Sundar Pichai says it will improve the web.

I’m not sure about that one…

Nobody wants to read bland, boring AI content.

But the whole débâcle reeks of automated plagiarism, too.

Who gave Google permission to use content that publishers invested time and money into creating for its own product?

And that’s only one type of plagiarism to watch out for online these days.

Write on,

Bryan Collins

title: Watch out for Twiddlers!
html:
Hi Reader,

I sold one of my food and drinks websites last week for a small loss.

And all because of a Twiddler.

I started this web project two years ago. I picked up an old food and drinks web domain from domain brokerage ODYS. This web domain has authority, links, and a catchy name.

Then, I installed Astra, a WordPress theme for food and drink bloggers. I approached this site like a cooker project. I decided to publish 50–60 food and drink articles and let them stew.

I researched some keywords for these articles but didn’t want to write that much content myself. So, I hired a food and drinks writer to write this content.

I gave him a spreadsheet of keywords, and off he went. His content was all I’d expect from a foodie. I spent little time or money on the site beyond paying this writer.

This strategy–publishing relevant content on expired domains–worked well for a few years. Following this approach, I built up traffic for several other websites.

Not anymore.

Traffic for my cooker project trended downward since the Google Helpful Content Update last September. So, I let the writer go and my content site for a few months. I hoped my traffic stats would turn around.

Well, hope isn’t a content strategy.

Info about the Google algorithm leaked on May 24th. SEO X worked itself into a frenzy about information from a 2,500-page document. Much of the leak contradicts the vanilla advice from Google’s reps about how search works.

An example? Google reps say new sites don’t have to wait in a sandbox for a few months before ranking. Write content readers like, and you’ll get traffic.

Well, it turns out a sandbox exists for new sites. And site owners must wait.

That’s one of the Twiddlers in this 2,500-page document. These Twiddlers classify a site for the algorithm.

Another Twiddler classifies sites as small or personal projects, such as blogs. This Twiddler may explain how Google is killing off many smaller sites and reserving space in the SERPS for its friends at Forbes, Quora, and Reddit.

The Google algo pushes content for smaller sites and bloggers down the results page. Our traffic overlords at Google can turn one of those Twiddlers and crash a site simply because it’s not big enough.

A Twiddler doesn’t care how much you or a writer knows about home brewing, travel, cats, or [insert niche of choice].

Why am I telling you all this?

Perhaps you don’t care about niche websites, SEO or even Twiddlers.

Well, many writers still want to publish content on their personal sites, but they’re wondering if blogging is dead.

Pro Writers shouldn’t depend on any ONE platform for connecting with followers, readers, and potential clients.

You could be knee-deep in SEO only for Google to turn one of its Twiddlers and tank your site.

You could be building a massive Insta account only for Meta to kill your profile’s reach in favor of pay-for-play.

Or you could be publishing books on KDP only for Amazon to prioritize book advertisers.

So, I’m treating my main site like any social media platform.

I’ll still write and publish content on it, but I don’t expect a reliable stream of traffic. So, I’ll diversify.

I’ll also write and publish on one or two key social media platforms where I can connect with clients, but I won’t depend on them.

I want readers to join my email list instead. It’s an insurance policy against an algo change or a Twiddler.

I’d like to invite you to a Pro Writers Only workshop on this topic. How to Start a 6-Figure Newsletter Business. Buy a ticket.

Write on,
Bryan Collins

title: How to start a newsletter business
html:
Hi Reader,

My email list contains two types of readers.

And they'll sacrifice their firstborn to do it.

They sometimes reply, in ALL CAPS, looking for cash.

Last week, I wrote about getting paid $573.75 for writing one email.

Pressing send on that email was like hitting a wasp's nest with a honey-covered stick.

The first type of reader responded en masse.

I could have written to them about dropshipping or trading crypto versus starting a newsletter business.

"Just tell me how I can earn it, " one reader demanded.

Another wanted to send me his bank details.

Another insisted we chat about payment on WhatsApp urgently.

The funny thing is I included a video in the same email explaining my newsletter strategy.

Now, the other half of my list?

They're interested in building a writing business.

And they get that running a newsletter is ONE way to earn money from writing.

But it's not a quick fix.

A newsletter owner still needs to start their newsletter, build their list, and write publicly every day (or at least every week).

In other words, sweat equity is required.

How to Start a 6-Figure Newsletter Business

title: The hidden weapon in my copywriting arsenal
html:
Hi Reader,

I’m a collector.

Over the years, I’ve collected comic books, rare coins, old books, printables, audio speakers, digital artworks, marathon training shoes, and copywriting frameworks.

I don’t keep all my collections.

I binned my tattered, yellow comic book collection and gave away my moldy rare coins years ago. I sold my old speakers and donated my running shoes.

I only hold onto valuable collections I either use regularly or enjoy.

Balancing collecting and minimalism is always challenging!

After parting with my rare coins and comics, I spent a few years taking copywriting courses and working with clients.

While honing my “write words that sell” chops, I collected copywriting frameworks for headlines, sales hooks, and bullets.

I took them from books, courses, sales pages, and marketing campaigns.

I stuffed them all into a digital swipe file because I’ve a mortal fear of the flashing cursor and an unreasonable client deadline.

My copywriting swipe file saved me hours when I worked as an in-house copywriter for a SaaS company. I still use my swipe file to write sales pages for my business.

One Friday morning, a client asked me to turn around some sales copy for a deadline. And he needed it that afternoon.

Charming.

I waded through my swipe file of copywriting frameworks.

I pulled out a proven framework and worked it into my copy.

The client signed off on the copy. He likened my writing process to “voodoo magic.”

(I’d the same response after watching a developer fix a broken app by writing a few lines of code in several minutes.)

You see…

Understand copywriting, and you gain a huge advantage over most writers, marketers, and business owners.

They’re stuck with bland vanilla outputs from ChatGPT that most won’t read, let alone act on.

YOU can write words that sell.

Take the humble copywriting bullet.

A good copywriting bullet is powerful enough to sell a product or service by itself.

They’re also a great way of making a sales page pop.

Clients and prospects love them.

Picking product features and turning them into bullets is a great way of honing your copywriting skills.

Here are a few examples:

  • How to land your first copywriting client EVEN if you have no experience
  • Big mistakes new copywriters make about niche selection
  • The one network copywriters MUST USE to find high-paying clients
  • 3 surprisingly easy methods for pitching high-paying clients
  • The best way to set rates with your copywriting clients
  • How to relieve prospect’s objections when pitching your copywriting services
  • A simple trick you can use to increase your copywriting rates
  • Got one hour? Here are 3 things you must do for your copywriting business
  • How to turn features into benefits… your clients will love it!
  • What should always do after a client pays you
  • The big lie about using AI to become a copywriter
  • And that’s just a sample of the many techniques you can use to build a copywriting business

See if you can spot a few frameworks in that list and turn them into bullets for your current project.

If you enjoy that, I recommend copywriting as a great way for Pro Writers who want to earn a good living.

title: Writers Need More Than 1 Income Stream
html:
Hi Reader,

In 2008, I relied on one income stream.

Freelance writing.

When the banks stuck dynamite on the Irish economy, my income went with ka-boom.

I spent a few months on social welfare.

I figured earning a living from writing was too hard.

So I almost quit.

Then, I took a few courses, worked with a mentor, and (accidentally) started a writing business.

I discovered how to fix my pre-Great Recession mistake.

Pro writers don’t rely on one income stream, no matter how lucrative. They build multiple income streams, each a little finger on the hand that is their business.

You see…

Going all in with a single client or business model is too risky. You need an insurance policy.

Sure, freelancing is fun, but what happens when your client can’t or won’t pay up? Or when a VP suddenly kills next month’s budget for freelancers?

Over the years, I built up several income streams from writing online.

I tried freelancing again but this time around the margins of a day job.

I wrote articles and sales copy for business owners.

I spent some of the week on client work and some pitching new clients. Insurance policy secured.

Later, I self-published over a dozen non-fiction books on Amazon, Kobo, and via my website.

At one point, my non-fiction books earned several thousand dollars a month.

I recently read about a LitRPG indie author earning six figures… a month.

The self-publishing business model can still work, but top indie authors also sell directly to readers, create multiple book formats like audible and print, and invest in ads.

I formed affiliate partnerships with brands and companies I like.

Then, I created content about their products and services.

This was insanely profitable for a few years. Affiliate marketing is harder now, thanks to a series of brutal Google algo updates.

You’ll find a lot of affiliate marketers lurking sub-Reddits ready to deploy their lousy AI content spinners.

I built my site up to millions of pageviews with SEO.

I used profits from my other income streams to hire a team of writers.

Then, I monetised my site by running ads on my site.

These ads earn money as long as my sites get traffic. That’s as close to passive income as I managed.

I created and sold online writing courses.

These writing courses still sell well today. It’s a straightforward business model if you can marry what you teach to your audience.

However, many students and clients don’t want more videos to scrub through on X2 or another library of Teachable courses they’ll never log in to.

They prefer access to the teacher or mentor.

That’s more time-intensive for you. And it means less time writing.

I also run sponsored slots for my daily newsletter.

They don’t earn as much as some of the other revenue streams listed above. But I get paid for writing emails that I’m sending anyway.

My email marketing provider hooks me up with sponsors.

Not all my attempts at building new income streams worked out.

I had less success flipping niche content websites and selling writing printables and other writing tools.

These are a few of the ways you can monetize your writing.

So, where to start?

The easiest way to combine these income streams is with a newsletter or email list.

Then, you can promote your latest books, courses, and products to your list.

It brings each income stream together. And it’s fun to write, too.

Write on,
Bryan Collins

title: If I went broke, I'd get paid to write like this
html:
Hi Reader,

As part of this series on building a writing business, I’ve covered why email newsletters are non-negotiable for your writing business.

And I’ve explained why I’d write on owned and earned platforms.

TL;DR: LinkedIn is like Bumble for writers who need clients. Get on it!

Money will find you if you grow a healthy email list from LinkedIn or elsewhere.

As an example:

My email lists have around 25,000 subscribers.

I get multiple emails from ConvertKit connecting me with potential sponsors every month.

They pay to appear in this newsletter.

I don’t accept them all.

But if they’re a good fit, ConvertKit gives me a snippet for the sponsor.

I simply write my email, insert the snippet and click send.

ConvertKit pays me a few weeks later.

Remember, I’m sending this email ad or no ad.

Beehiiv offers a similar sponsorship service.

Or you can do all this manually and reach out to potential advertisers.

(I tried this and found it too time-intensive.)

Newsletter sponsorships are a nice side-earner, but they’re not enough to build a sustainable writing business.

I’d also create a service, a product, or consulting that I can sell rather than relying on a partner network or advertiser.

I’d pitch these early and often to connections and subscribers. Otherwise, writing online is simply a hobby and a business.

And we’re not in the business of treating writing like a hobby!

You can sell services like ghostwriting or copywriting to clients, whereby you get paid to create content for them.

I worked as a copywriter for years, and it’s lucrative.

In fact, I regularly help clients find work as a copywriter because they learn how to write words that sell.

And it pays more than freelancing.

I found it hard to scale this work without hiring others and starting an agency.

Enter digital products.

I’ve created dozens of digital products, including templates, tools, courses, and even books.

(Yes, books are products.)

Creating a digital course sounds like the ultimate passive income stream. Create once. Sell many times.

But I’ve found that customers today want access to the creator, not another 6 hours of video to watch on x2.

I’ve often paid over the odds for a 60-minute mentorship 1:1 call instead of another premium online course.

I prefer offering consultancy or coaching services, whereby followers buy my time, and I solve a problem for them.

Plus, I prefer talking directly to customers and clients.

Consultancy and coaching work well once your list gains momentum. You can offer group calls and also charge more for direct access.

Whatever your approach, don’t forget job number one.

Grow your email list. Engage with your subscribers. Make regular offers.

Follow that checklist, and you’ll get paid to write.

It’s one I still follow today.

title: I cry a little every time I open X
html:
Hi Reader,

This week, I’m explaining how I’d build a writing business if I started over.

Yesterday, I wrote about why an email newsletter is the cornerstone of a profitable writing business.

Ideally, craft a personality-driven newsletter for an ideal reader.

You own platforms like your email list, newsletter, or website.

They’re a nice insurance policy against the algo and our future AI overloads.

They can take my reach, impressions, and followers, but they’ll never take my email list!

I loved writing on owned platforms.

I’ve spent dozens of hours going through the owned platforms of big-name online writers with SEO tools like SEMRush.

Alas, I’m a geeky outlier.

Growing on an owned platform is harder now than in 2014, even if you’ve got rock-solid SEO chops.

Like it or not, a good chunk of your audience is swiping madly on Insta instead of reading immaculately crafted content on some random person’s website.

We’re fighting in a battle for people’s attention.

So, I’d also write and publish content on one earned platform daily.

I’d earn people’s attention… and their best email addresses by writing, creating content, and asking them explicitly to join my list.

I’d pick one platform for finding clients and bringing money into my writing business.

The problem?

Writing on social media is like stepping into a battleground.

Hustle X is full of wantrepreneurs hawking their subscriber counts, Notion templates, and monthly recurring revenue stats.

Kudos!

With all that social flexing, good luck reaching your followers, never mind pitching a service.

And that’s before Elon decides to fire the other half of X or tweak the algo for some vanity project.

Some writers are crushing it on Insta with text-based photos and heavily scripted reels.

I tried that for a while.

It wasn’t for me.

Spending hours writing short-form content frazzled my brain.

Those CEOs who need help with their content strategy?

They’re not doom scrolling TikTok!

Here’s the answer:

LinkedIn is hot right now for creators who can write valuable content.

You’re also far more likely to connect with and find paying clients.

It’s the perfect network for building a profitable writing business.

So, I’d publish content from my newsletter on LinkedIn several times a week.

I’d use a tool like Taplio to write and schedule my content in advance because being plugged into the grid 24/7 is a recipe for burnout.

I’d send connection requests to 5–10 people per day.

I’d ask new followers to join my email list.

I’d all but ignore the other networks.

Sure, it’s a grind.

But War. War never changes.

With my content strategy in place, I’d monetize.
